summary.text: Assuming only finitely many such primes, injectivity of \(x\mapsto x^4+1\) bounds every admissible base \(x=\phi(p)\phi(q)\) by some \(K\). Positivity then gives every \(n>2\) a decomposition \(n=p+q\), but \(\phi(p)=p-1\), positivity of the totients, and the elementary bound \(q\le 2\phi(q)^2\) imply \(p\le K+1\) and \(q\le 2K^2\), uniformly bounding all such \(n\) and yielding a contradiction.

full_proof.text:
Let \(\phi\) denote Euler's totient function. For each positive integer \(n\), let \(a(n)\) count the primes \(p<n\) for which, on writing
\[
q=n-p>0,
\]
the number
\[
\bigl(\phi(p)\phi(q)\bigr)^4+1
\]
is also prime. Assume that
\[
a(n)>0\qquad\text{for every }n>2.
\]
We prove that there are infinitely many primes of the form \(x^4+1\).

We first establish the estimate on Euler's totient function that will be needed later:
\[
 m\le 2\phi(m)^2                                                   \tag{1}
\]
for every positive integer \(m\). In fact, if \(m\) is odd, the stronger estimate
\[
 m\le \phi(m)^2                                                     \tag{2}
\]
holds.

To prove these estimates, first consider a prime power \(p^r\), where \(r\ge 1\). The standard prime-power formula for the totient is
\[
\phi(p^r)=p^{r-1}(p-1).
\]
Indeed, among the \(p^r\) residue classes modulo \(p^r\), exactly the \(p^{r-1}\) multiples of \(p\) fail to be coprime to \(p^r\), leaving \(p^r-p^{r-1}=p^{r-1}(p-1)\) coprime classes.

Suppose first that \(p\) is odd. Then \(p\ge 3\), and
\[
p\le (p-1)^2.
\]
Also, because \(r\ge 1\), we have \(p^{r-1}\le p^{2r-2}\). Therefore
\[
 p^r=p^{r-1}p
 \le p^{r-1}(p-1)^2
 \le p^{2r-2}(p-1)^2
 =\phi(p^r)^2.                                                     \tag{3}
\]
For the prime \(2\), the formula gives \(\phi(2^r)=2^{r-1}\), and hence
\[
2\phi(2^r)^2=2\cdot 2^{2r-2}=2^{2r-1}\ge 2^r,                    \tag{4}
\]
since \(r\le 2r-1\).

Now factor a positive integer \(m\) into prime powers. Euler's totient is multiplicative on coprime factors: if \(u\) and \(v\) are coprime, then
\[
\phi(uv)=\phi(u)\phi(v).
\]
This follows, for example, from the correspondence between residue classes modulo \(uv\) and pairs of residue classes modulo \(u\) and \(v\), under which a class is coprime to \(uv\) exactly when its two components are coprime to \(u\) and \(v\), respectively.

If \(m\) is odd, all of its prime-power factors involve odd primes. Multiplying (3) over those pairwise coprime prime-power factors and using multiplicativity gives
\[
m\le \phi(m)^2,
\]
which is (2). This also covers \(m=1\), where both sides are \(1\).

If \(m\) is even, write \(m=2^r u\), where \(r\ge 1\) and \(u\) is odd. The two factors are coprime. Combining (4) with the odd estimate for \(u\), we obtain
\[
 m=2^r u
 \le 2\phi(2^r)^2\phi(u)^2
 =2\bigl(\phi(2^r)\phi(u)\bigr)^2
 =2\phi(m)^2.
\]
Thus (1) holds for every positive \(m\).

We now argue by contradiction. Let
\[
S=\{\ell\in\mathbb N:\ \ell\text{ is prime and }\ell=x^4+1
       \text{ for some }x\in\mathbb N\}.
\]
Suppose that \(S\) is finite.

Consider the set of possible fourth-power bases producing members of \(S\):
\[
T=\{x\in\mathbb N:x^4+1\in S\}.
\]
The map
\[
f:\mathbb N\longrightarrow\mathbb N,\qquad f(x)=x^4+1,
\]
is injective. Indeed, the fourth-power map is strictly increasing on the nonnegative integers, so \(u^4+1=v^4+1\) implies \(u=v\). Consequently, the inverse image under \(f\) of the finite set \(S\) is finite; equivalently, \(T\) is finite. Every finite set of nonnegative integers is bounded above, so there is some \(K\in\mathbb N\) such that
\[
x\le K\qquad\text{for every }x\in T.                             \tag{5}
\]

We will show that this single number \(K\) gives a uniform upper bound for every integer \(n>2\), which is impossible.

Fix any \(n>2\). By the assumed positivity \(a(n)>0\), at least one admissible decomposition counted by \(a(n)\) exists. Thus there is a prime \(p<n\), and, with
\[
q=n-p,
\]
we have \(q>0\) and
\[
R=\bigl(\phi(p)\phi(q)\bigr)^4+1
\]
is prime. Set
\[
x=\phi(p)\phi(q).
\]
Then \(R=x^4+1\) is prime, so \(R\in S\), and hence \(x\in T\). By (5),
\[
\phi(p)\phi(q)\le K.                                               \tag{6}
\]

Because \(p\) is prime, \(p>0\), and because \(q>0\), both totients \(\phi(p)\) and \(\phi(q)\) are positive integers. In particular each is at least \(1\). It follows from (6) that each factor is itself at most \(K\):
\[
\phi(p)\le K,
\qquad
\phi(q)\le K.                                                      \tag{7}
\]
More explicitly, \(\phi(q)\ge1\) gives
\(\phi(p)\le\phi(p)\phi(q)\le K\), and \(\phi(p)\ge1\) gives
\(\phi(q)\le\phi(p)\phi(q)\le K\).

For a prime \(p\), one has \(\phi(p)=p-1\). The first inequality in (7) therefore yields
\[
p-1\le K,
\qquad\text{so}\qquad
p\le K+1.                                                         \tag{8}
\]
Applying the totient estimate (1) to the positive integer \(q\), and then using the second inequality in (7), gives
\[
q\le2\phi(q)^2\le2K^2.                                            \tag{9}
\]
Since \(n=p+q\), inequalities (8) and (9) imply
\[
n=p+q\le K+1+2K^2.                                                \tag{10}
\]
The important point is that \(K\) came only from the assumed finite set \(S\), not from \(n\). Thus (10) says that every natural number \(n>2\) is bounded above by the same constant
\[
B=K+1+2K^2.
\]

This is impossible. For example, take
\[
n=B+3=K+1+2K^2+3.
\]
Certainly \(n>2\), so (10) would give \(B+3\le B\), a contradiction.

Therefore the supposition that \(S\) is finite is false. Hence there are infinitely many primes \(\ell\) for which
\[
\ell=x^4+1
\]
for some nonnegative integer \(x\), as required.
